transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I’ve been hearing my name called. At home, it sounds like it’s coming from the hallway, and once at the warehouse too—but nobody was there. It sounds as real as my husband standing right next to me, and that scared me.
How long have you been hearing your name called like this—days, weeks, or longer?

It’s been happening long enough that it scared me into coming in. I hear my name from the hallway at home, and it happened once at the warehouse too. It sounds completely real, like my husband is right beside me.
Have you been using any alcohol, marijuana, or other recreational drugs recently, or taken any new medications around the time this started?
I’m not really sure what would count. I haven’t noticed anything different around when it started.
Thinking back to when you first started hearing your name called like this, how many days or weeks ago did it begin?
About three weeks, I think. The whole change—from feeling wound up and restless, to hearing my name, then crashing—has been going on that long.
Do you hear your name being called only when you're feeling really wound up or really down, or does it also happen during times when your mood feels normal?

Only when I was really wound up, I think—barely sleeping, talking nonstop, feeling like I had to fix everything. I didn’t have the voice before that, and I haven’t had it since I dropped into that low, withdrawn time.

latest_inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (hearing name called) occur exclusively during manic phase (elevated, restless, non-stop talking) and resolve with mood shift to depressive/withdrawn state, indicating mood-congruent/incongruent psychotic features tied to a manic episode rather than an independent psychotic disorder. This pattern of psychosis strictly confined to mood episodes rules out schizophrenia spectrum disorders (F20.9, F28, F29), schizoaffective disorder (F25.0, which requires psychosis without mood symptoms for a period), substance-induced psychosis (F19.951, no substance use reported), and organic psychotic disorder (F06.0, no medical cause identified). The 3-week history of cycling from manic to depressive symptoms with psychosis only in the manic phase supports Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic with psychotic features.
